episode_title: Language Truly is PPE: Language Risk Mitigation on the Jobsite

real_qa.q: What percentage of job-related construction accidents does OSHA attribute to language barriers?
real_qa.r: OSHA says 25 percent of job-related accidents are attributed to language barriers. However, Monique Lewis notes this number is likely underreported, as many incidents go unreported entirely when workers lack the language to report them or don't feel safe doing so.
real_qa.requete: OSHA language barrier job accidents percentage

real_qa.q: What percentage of Hispanic workers does Monique Lewis observe on construction job sites compared to official statistics?
real_qa.r: Official numbers tell us 33 percent of construction workers are Hispanic, but Monique Lewis observes when passing work zones daily that she is seeing 50 to 60 percent Hispanic faces on construction sites, suggesting the actual demographic presence is significantly higher than reported statistics.

real_qa.q: How long did it take a safety director to see measurable improvement after joining Monique Lewis's language training program?
real_qa.r: A safety director who had worked with a Spanish-speaking crew for about six months was only in Monique Lewis's program for about seven weeks. During that time, he was able to recognize and address a situation where a Hispanic worker reported his harness had been damaged and he had needed one for months but lacked the English comfort level to report it.
real_qa.requete: construction safety language training seven weeks results

real_qa.q: What is Next2Native's mission regarding language in construction safety?
real_qa.r: Next2Native's mission is to bring language to the same level of importance in the construction industry's mind as a hard hat. The company operates under the theme that language is PPE (personal protective equipment), and language truly is PPE because it protects workers just as much as physical equipment does.

real_qa.q: What bilingual communication gap exists in construction toolbox talks and OSHA training delivery?
real_qa.r: Many companies conduct toolbox talks and OSHA trainings entirely in English without bilingual instruction available. Monique Lewis describes a case where an OSHA instructor delivered fall protection training completely in English to a crew that included three Spanish-speaking Hispanic workers; all gave thumbs up at the end, but moments later one worker tied a rope around his waist and climbed to height—revealing he had not understood the training.
real_qa.requete: OSHA training Spanish speaking workers language barrier

real_qa.q: Why does using a bilingual foreman alone not fully solve language barriers on construction job sites?
real_qa.r: A bilingual foreman acting as the sole translator for 30 to 50 percent of a crew becomes overwhelmed, unable to perform their primary job duties, and their mental bandwidth is consumed by translating. Additionally, they become aware of private HR issues they should not know about, and if an injured non-English speaker needs medical care, the foreman leaves the crew without a liaison.
real_qa.requete: bilingual foreman language barrier construction limitations

guest.bio_context: Monique Lewis is a language risk strategist and founder of Next2Native, serving the construction industry. She is the only bilingual English-Spanish keynote speaker currently addressing language safety in construction. She learned Spanish over 20 years ago and pivoted her company to focus on construction after learning about a fatality on a construction site in Charlotte, North Carolina, where language barriers played a critical role.

real_quote: Language truly is PPE. So we are working toward our mission to bring it to that same level in the minds of our industry as a whole, so that it is looked at just as necessary and baseline as a hard hat.
key_stats: OSHA: 25 percent of job-related construction accidents attributed to language barriers
Official statistics show 33 percent Hispanic representation in construction, but Monique Lewis observes 50 to 60 percent on actual job sites
Women represent 11 percent of construction industry workforce
Safety director showed measurable improvement results within seven weeks of language training program
Monique Lewis based in Raleigh, North Carolina
Monique Lewis has over 20 years of experience in Spanish language and construction industry expertise
